tier_reason: The SamSaffron/allocator_bench README shows lockless 1.4 against the built-in glibc malloc with public scripts (stress_mem.rb, test_all.rb, LD_PRELOAD per allocator), but no CPU model, compiler or flags, single unrepeated runs, and a small personal repo (56 stars) rather than a well-known suite, so it falls short of A and of a B-grade independent suite; the vendor's own benchmark page is first-party and was egress-blocked.

corrections.claimed_speedup: SamSaffron/allocator_bench (Ruby 2.6.5, lockless 1.4 versus built-in glibc malloc): 8 threads 2.859 s versus 3.423 s (1.20x faster, derived from page data) with RSS 249,540 KB versus 186,336 KB (34% more, the highest RSS of every allocator in that run); 1 thread 2.874 s versus 3.296 s (1.15x faster, derived from page data) with RSS 164,468 KB versus 169,444 KB. Older runs: Ruby 2.5.1, lockless 1.4 3.568 s versus 4.928 s (1.38x, derived from page data); Ruby 2.3.3, lockless 1.3 3.689 s versus 5.463 s (1.48x, derived from page data). Lockless is mid-pack among the alternatives: at 8 threads tcmalloc 2.5 (2.764 s), tcmalloc 2.0 (2.797 s), rpmalloc (2.824 s) and jemalloc 5.2.0 (2.837 s) are faster and jemalloc 5.2.1 is within 2% (2.922 s); at 1 thread tcmalloc 2.6.3 (2.526 s) and several other tcmalloc/jemalloc versions are faster. The vendor's own page (blocked, snippet only) compares against eglibc 2.11, nedmalloc 1.06, hoard 3.8, jemalloc 2.2.1 and tcmalloc 1.7 with the t-test1 benchmark.
corrections.caveats: Evidence is one personal Ruby benchmark repo (SamSaffron/allocator_bench, public scripts, last commit 2020-07-06) with no CPU model, compiler or flags stated, so tier C; the results are single runs without variance. The workload is Ruby string allocation under the GVL, so the '8 threads' runs do not allocate truly in parallel and the allocator margin is small (1.15 to 1.48x); lockless also used the most memory of any allocator at 8 threads (34% more RSS than glibc). Many tcmalloc and jemalloc versions match or beat it. The vendor page https://locklessinc.com/benchmarks_allocator.shtml and the whole locklessinc.com domain (including mail.locklessinc.com) are egress-blocked, so vendor numbers (t-test1 versus eglibc 2.11, nedmalloc 1.06, hoard 3.8, jemalloc 2.2.1, tcmalloc 1.7) are known from search snippets only. Licence GPL-3.0-or-later is confirmed from the vendor README and ll_alloc.c header carried in the GitHub mirror jl2922/lockless_allocator ('GPL version 3 (or any later version)'; commercial licences offered by the vendor); the source copyright reads 2009-2011, and the vendor what's-new page (snippet only) lists the last allocator update on 23 Jul 2012 (aligned_alloc support), so the code is effectively abandoned. GPL means linking obliges source redistribution.

notes: All README numbers match the page; I added the Ruby 2.3.3 row and the fact that lockless is mid-pack (several tcmalloc versions, rpmalloc and jemalloc 5.2.0 are faster) and has the highest 8-thread RSS. Licence GPL-3.0-or-later now confirmed via the jl2922/lockless_allocator mirror; maintenance set to abandoned from the 2009-2011 source copyright and a what's-new snippet (last allocator update July 2012). Shortcomings: small Ruby-dominated margin, GVL-serialised threads, no hardware/compiler, single runs, vendor page blocked.

tier_reason: First-party docs page with public benchmark code (benchmarks/sum_libcsp.c, benchmarks/sum_go.go, benchmarks/Makefile with CFLAGS -Wall -O3, GCC 8.3.0, Go 1.14) but the CPU model is not stated (only 8 cores, 8192 MB, Linux 4.15.0-88-generic), so not A.

corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark with public code (benchmarks/sum_libcsp.c, sum_go.go, sum_thread.c and benchmarks/Makefile), but the CPU model is not stated; the environment is listed only as 8 cores, 8192 MB, Linux ubuntu-bionic 4.15.0-88-generic (the hostname and round memory size suggest a VM, not confirmed). The workload is a pure process-spawn microbenchmark (two child processes per node, about 20 million per round) with no cutoff, so it measures create-schedule-destroy overhead rather than real applications; the Go side allocates two closures and a WaitGroup per node that escape to the heap, so Go's GC and growable-stack costs are included, while libcsp's stacks are sized at compile time by its GCC plugin and 'cspcli analyze' (the memory column reflects that static sizing). Building needs the libcsp GCC plugin plus the cspcli analysis step with a fixed core count. Go 1.14 dates from 2020; no newer Go was tested. The pthread comparison could not run at the same size: sum_thread.c comments say MAX had to be cut to 10,000 (3.2 s per round) because 10^7 exceeds the Linux thread limit. LICENSE file is MIT while source headers carry ISC-style permission text (both OSI-permissive). Single author; last commit 2023-06-30, so abandoned.

notes: All eight libcsp/Go timings and the memory column match the docs page (ratios 10.2x, 13.2x, 11.1x correctly derived). Metadata verified: 1.3k stars, MIT, last commit 2023-06-30 (abandoned). Shortcomings: CPU model missing, spawn-only microbenchmark versus untuned Go 1.14 code, GCC-plugin build requirement.

tier_reason: contrib/psota-benchmark/results.txt with the public script contrib/psota-benchmark/tcp.sh states gcc 4.2.2, the Gentoo CFLAGS and the CPU models, so it is mechanically A-reproducible, but it shows libarchive not faster overall (slower create and extract on all four data sets, list faster on only two) with 2007 versions, so C is kept as a documentation entry rather than a speed win.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Mixed, mostly not faster. 64-bit Athlon 64 X2, tmpfs, Linux 2.6.23 tree (291 MB, best of 5): list 0.164 s versus GNU tar 0.218 s (bsdtar 1.33x faster, derived from page data); create 0.764 s versus 0.743 s (GNU tar 1.03x faster); extract 0.733 s versus 0.625 s (GNU tar 1.17x faster). 64-bit, disk, 3.2 GB in 7,447 files (best of 3): list 0.053 s versus 56.535 s (unexplained, since the script passes --seek to GNU tar); create 184.680 s versus 159.240 s (GNU tar 1.16x faster); extract 78.914 s versus 78.480 s (tie). 32-bit 1.5 GHz Athlon, drivers tree (119 MB, best of 3): list 0.167 s versus 0.161 s, create 1.329 s versus 1.223 s, extract 1.186 s versus 1.064 s (GNU tar faster in all three). 32-bit, disk, 2.1 GB (best of 3): list 0.214 s versus 0.210 s, create 182.171 s versus 174.999 s, extract 94.912 s versus 94.657 s (GNU tar marginally faster in all three). Tim Kientzle's note attributes bsdtar's list wins to lseek() skipping over entry bodies, which GNU tar also offers. The project itself only claims 'efficient'.
corrections.workload: Jan Psota's TCP script (tcp.sh) timing bsdtar (libarchive 2.3.4), GNU tar 1.19 and star 1.5a85 creating, listing and extracting a pax-format archive; four data sets on two machines: Linux 2.6.23 source (291 MB, 23,867 files) on tmpfs, best of 5, and a 3.2 GB home directory on reiserfs disk on a 64-bit Athlon 64 X2; a 119 MB driver tree and a 2.1 GB home directory on a 32-bit Athlon, best of 3.
corrections.caveats: Not a speed claim by the project: the data is a 2007 mailing-list post by a third party (Jan Psota, Bug-tar list), archived in contrib/psota-benchmark with the TCP script (tcp.sh) beside it; the committed script sets n=3 while the first result set says best of 5. Versions are libarchive 2.3.4 and GNU tar 1.19, so the numbers are stale by almost twenty years. The 'compare' rows are invalid: Tim Kientzle's note says bsdtar does not support that operation (the script does not abort on its failure), so its 0.001 s is a no-op. bsdtar is slower than GNU tar for create and extract on all four data sets; its list win appears on the two 64-bit sets only and comes from lseek() skipping, a feature GNU tar has too; the script passes --seek to GNU tar, so the 1000x list gap on the 3.2 GB disk run is not explained by the file. Covers only uncompressed archives; compressed or tape cases are untested. Licence: COPYING is a 2-clause BSD notice for most sources, with a few files under 3-clause UC Regents, public domain or CC0/OpenSSL/Apache-2.0, all permissive. Filed so the shortcoming is recorded; libarchive is not shown to be faster than GNU tar overall.

notes: All quoted numbers match results.txt; I added the 32-bit machine sets (GNU tar faster or tied in every create, list and extract) and the 64-bit disk create/extract rows, so the list win holds on only two of four sets. Metadata verified: 3.6k stars, BSD-2-Clause COPYING, last commit 2026-10-06 (active). Keep as a documented not-faster entry: shortcomings are stale 2007 versions, slower create/extract, a no-op compare row, and a list-only win from lseek skipping.
